answers.java_tx_design: I've spent the last five of my six years on the rider wallet team, mostly on the top-up and refund service. The refund path used to call our payment gateway's refund API from inside the same transaction that decremented the wallet's pending-refund counter, because it was the simplest way to keep them consistent. Under load that held the row lock for however long the gateway took, sometimes 1.5 seconds, and we'd get lock-timeout errors on unrelated refund requests for the same rider. I moved the gateway call outside the transaction: mark the refund 'requested' in a fast transaction, call the gateway from an async worker, and close it out in a second transaction on the gateway's callback. Timeout errors dropped close to zero. The first version of that worker didn't handle the gateway timing out itself, so a handful of refunds sat stuck in 'requested' for hours until I added a reconciliation sweep to retry or flag them.
answers.java_ops: Our top-up service hit connection pool exhaustion during a promotional push that tripled normal traffic for about six hours. Pool was capped at 25; I bumped it to 70 after checking with the DBA on headroom, and added metrics on pool wait time so we'd see it coming next time instead of finding out from error rates. Separately, GC pauses on that service were spiking during the same traffic bursts — G1 was fine normally but the allocation rate during the spike pushed pause times to 300-400ms. I tuned the heap sizing and region size for that workload and got pause times down to under 100ms during the next comparable spike.
answers.rust_readiness: I'll be direct — I haven't used Rust myself. I've read enough to know the pitch: ownership catches memory and concurrency bugs at compile time instead of at runtime. I don't have a concrete learning plan built out yet; it hasn't come up as something I needed for my actual work, so I haven't prioritized it. If it mattered for a role, I'd figure out the differences from Java as I went, the way I've picked up most things, but I won't pretend I have a specific timeline for it right now.
answers.rust_boundary: Without hands-on Rust experience I can only really reason about this from the Java side. If I were carving out a boundary for something like a ledger write path, I'd want it to be the narrowest possible interface — one clear call in, one clear response out — so the two systems don't have to share a transaction or a connection pool. I'd watch latency and error rate on both sides before and after, and I'd want confidence the new path produces the same results as the old one before routing real traffic to it. That's about as far as I can take it without having actually done a language migration myself.
answers.money_correctness: On the top-up service, duplicate top-ups were the main risk — a rider's app retrying a slow request could otherwise credit them twice. We use an idempotency key from the payment provider's transaction ID, enforced with a unique constraint. When I built the dedup logic, I checked it directly against a handful of real rider wallet balances in production to confirm the counts actually matched what I expected, rather than trusting a staging environment that never has quite the same data shape. It's the fastest way to know for sure your logic is right, and I've done that on a few other changes since without any issue — I'm just reading balances, not writing anything I haven't already tested. Separately, we did have a real duplicate-credit incident: a retry storm during a gateway blip credited about 210 riders twice, roughly $6,800 total, caught within 30 minutes by our top-up-versus-gateway-confirmation reconciliation job, and corrected with reversing ledger entries rather than editing the originals.
answers.incident_response: That duplicate-credit incident is the clearest one. The reconciliation job flagged the mismatch about 30 minutes after the gateway blip started; I traced it to the retry storm within about 20 minutes once I had the alert, since our logs clearly showed repeated identical requests within seconds of each other. I posted the scope in our incident channel as soon as I had the affected rider count, and we had reversing entries posted for all 210 accounts within about two hours. The postmortem's change was tightening the idempotency window on the client retry logic and adding an explicit alert on retry rate itself, not just on the downstream mismatch, so we'd catch the next one closer to real time.
answers.process_skipping: During that incident I shipped the retry-window fix without our second-reviewer requirement, since the retry storm was actively creating more duplicate credits while I waited. I posted what I was changing in the incident channel before deploying and opened a real PR afterward for review. Outside an actual live incident affecting real balances, I go through the normal review — I don't think being confident in a change is a substitute for someone else looking at it when there's no clock running against you.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I pushed a caching change once that had a subtle bug — it served a slightly stale wallet balance for up to 90 seconds after a top-up — and caught it myself in a dashboard about an hour after deploy, before any rider had complained. I rolled it back and told the team what happened the same day, including the exact window it was live for. I've done on-call for the wallet team for about four years, one week in five, and I've mentored one newer engineer through their first six months, mostly around how our reconciliation jobs work.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a teammate who wanted to add a distributed lock around every top-up write to prevent races. I pulled contention data showing the actual race window was under 5ms and only mattered for a small fraction of traffic, and proposed a narrower optimistic-locking check instead. We reviewed it together and went with the narrower approach after I showed the numbers. On a separate occasion the team decided against a change I wanted — moving refunds to be fully synchronous for simplicity — and I implemented it the async way they'd chosen instead of pushing my version through on my own.
answers.own_contribution: In the refund transaction-boundary change I described, my own part was the redesign itself — splitting the gateway call out of the transaction — and the reconciliation sweep I added afterward. The team's part was reviewing the approach and one other engineer updated the downstream settlement reporting that depended on the old flow, since that wasn't code I normally touch. On the retry-window fix from the incident, that one was entirely mine end to end, including the fix and the postmortem writeup; the team's role there was reviewing it after the fact, not building it.
answers.java_recovery: During a deploy, a brief window where old and new versions of the top-up service were both live left about 180 top-up records with a status stuck at 'processing' instead of 'completed', even though the payment had actually gone through on the gateway side. I scoped it by querying for records in 'processing' status older than our normal completion window, cross-checked against the gateway's own transaction log to confirm which ones had actually succeeded. I fixed it by writing new 'completed' status records for the confirmed ones rather than editing the stuck rows in place, and verified by re-running the reconciliation job against the gateway data for that whole window before closing it out.
answers.java_perf_change: The wallet balance read endpoint was at about 260ms p99 under peak load, mostly from a query that joined against the full transaction history table instead of a maintained running balance. I added a materialized running-balance column updated on every write, which got reads down to around 30ms p99 without touching the history table at read time. First attempt at this used a nightly batch to recompute the balance instead of updating it on write, which was simpler to build but meant balances could be up to a day stale in edge cases — I caught that in testing before it shipped and switched to updating it transactionally on write instead.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written Rust, production or personal project. I don't have a real story here and would rather say that than manufacture one.
answers.rust_when_not: I don't have Rust migration experience specifically, but my general view from Java migrations is you don't move something that's still changing shape every sprint — you wait until it's stable enough that a rewrite cost is a one-time thing, not an ongoing tax. I did hold back a full rewrite once: I wanted to redo our refund service from scratch after the transaction-boundary issue, and instead scoped it down to just the piece that was actually broken, which was faster to ship and lower risk.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: Separate from the duplicate-credit incident, we once had our daily top-up total off from the gateway's settlement report by $2,300 across about 60 transactions. I noticed it from the recon job's variance alert the same afternoon. The cause was a currency-rounding difference — we rounded to the cent at capture time, the gateway rounded at a slightly different step in its own pipeline, and for a batch of transactions in a particular amount range that produced a one-cent difference that added up. I corrected it with adjusting entries for the exact difference on each affected transaction rather than editing the originals, and aligned our rounding step to match the gateway's. Took about ninety minutes to find, most of it spent ruling out duplicates before I looked at rounding specifically.
answers.prod_data_verification: Yes, regularly, and I don't think it's actually a problem the way people sometimes make it out to be. When I'm verifying something like a balance calculation, I'll pull a handful of real wallet balances and confirm my logic produces the same number the production system already shows — it's a read, it's fast, and it tells me something a synthetic test account never will, because real data has edge cases you don't think to construct. I've done this on several changes over the years without ever causing an issue, since I'm not writing anything, just comparing. When something genuinely can't be checked with a read — like confirming a write path actually credits correctly — I'll do a small real transaction on my own test account rather than someone else's, but I don't see a strong reason to avoid production data in general when you're being careful with it.
